lead: Switch a DC source onto a circuit with one capacitor or one inductor and every voltage and current settles along the same exponential curve. The curve is the sum of two parts: a forced part set by the source and a natural part set by the energy already stored. Engineers use this split to read a datasheet, size a delay, or explain why a relay drops out late. This chapter shows the split, the one-line formula that joins the start and end values, and the sketches that follow from it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.2 for τ and the source-free exponential, and Unit 1 for KVL and KCL.

blocks.text: A first-order circuit has one storage element, so after switching its differential equation is first order. Its general solution has two pieces. The forced response (also called particular or steady-state response) is any solution that satisfies the driven equation and follows the source. The natural response (also called homogeneous, complementary or transient response) solves the source set to zero and always has the form A e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. The complete response is their sum.

For a constant DC source, the forced response is simply the final value x(∞), because after the exponential dies nothing changes. The natural part must carry the difference between the initial value x(0⁺) and that final value. Hence the shortcut:

blocks.where: x(t) is any current or voltage for t ≥ 0⁺; x(∞) is its steady value after the switch; x(0⁺) is its value just after switching; τ is the time constant, τ = R<sub>eq</sub>C or L/R<sub>eq</sub>, with R<sub>eq</sub> the resistance seen by the storage element with sources killed.

blocks.text: At t = 0⁺ the exponential equals 1, so x(0⁺) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]. As t → ∞ it goes to 0, so x → x(∞). The bracket is the initial mismatch. If x(0⁺) = x(∞), the natural part is zero and nothing changes.
For a series RC circuit with a DC voltage V<sub>s</sub> switched on at t = 0, KVL gives V<sub>s</sub> = R i + v<sub>C</sub> and i = C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt. With τ = RC,
v<sub>C</sub>(t) = V<sub>s</sub> + [v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) − V<sub>s</sub>] e<sup>−t/τ</sup>,   i(t) = [(V<sub>s</sub> − v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺))/R] e<sup>−t/τ</sup>
blocks.where: v<sub>C</sub> is capacitor voltage; i is series current; V<sub>s</sub> is the step voltage; v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) is the capacitor voltage just after switching. For an uncharged capacitor, v<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) and i = (V<sub>s</sub>/R)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. Capacitor voltage cannot jump, but capacitor current can: it jumps to (V<sub>s</sub> − v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺))/R at t = 0⁺ and decays to 0.

blocks.text: For a series RL circuit driven by V<sub>s</sub>, KVL gives V<sub>s</sub> = R i + L di/dt. With τ = L/R,
i(t) = I∞ + [i(0⁺) − I∞] e<sup>−t/τ</sup>,   I∞ = V<sub>s</sub>/R
blocks.where: i is inductor current; I∞ is its final value; i(0⁺) is inductor current just after switching. Inductor current cannot jump; inductor voltage v<sub>L</sub> = L di/dt can, and v<sub>L</sub>(t) = [V<sub>s</sub> − R i(0⁺)] e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. For zero initial current, i = (V<sub>s</sub>/R)(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) and v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>e<sup>−t/τ</sup>.

blocks.text: To sketch any first-order answer, mark x(0⁺) and x(∞) on the vertical axis. Draw an exponential from the first to the second. If x(∞) > x(0⁺), the curve rises; if x(∞) < x(0⁺), it falls. The initial slope is:

blocks.where: the slope has units of x per second; it is positive for a rising step and negative for a falling step. The tangent at t = 0 reaches the final value at t = τ. After 5τ the error is about 0.7% of the initial mismatch.

blocks.text: A pulse is two steps in the same circuit. First the source switches on at t = 0 and the answer runs toward its on-state final value. At t = T<sub>p</sub> it switches off, and the same formula restarts with x(T<sub>p</sub>⁺) as the new initial value and a new final value, often zero. If T<sub>p</sub> is much larger than τ, the capacitor or inductor fully charges and then fully discharges; if T<sub>p</sub> is much smaller than τ, it barely moves and the output looks like a distorted copy of the pulse. A repeating pulse train builds or droops according to this ratio.
With two storage elements the single exponential splits into two, covered in Chapter 5.4.

figure.caption: The flat line is the forced part; the falling curve is the natural part. Their sum is the rising capacitor voltage, which starts at 0 and ends at 1 normalised by V_s.

spec.aria: The flat forced response and the decaying natural response add up to the rising exponential of the total step response.

examples.question: A 10 V DC source is switched at t = 0 across a series combination of R = 50 kΩ and C = 2 μF. The capacitor is uncharged before switching. Find τ, v_C(t), i(t), and v_C at t = 0.1 s.
steps: For an uncharged capacitor, v_C(0⁺) = 0 V. After the transient, the capacitor is open to DC, so v_C(∞) = 10 V.
i(t) = C dv_C/dt = (2 × 10⁻⁶)(10)(10)e<sup>−10t</sup> A = 2 × 10⁻⁴ e<sup>−10t</sup> A = 0.2 e<sup>−10t</sup> mA.
examples.check:
import math
R = 50e3
C = 2e-6
Vs = 10.0
tau = R * C
vC_inf = Vs
vC_0 = 0.0
i0_mA = (Vs - vC_0) / R * 1000
t = 0.1
vC_t = vC_inf + (vC_0 - vC_inf) * math.exp(-t / tau)
print(round(tau, 3))
print(vC_inf)
print(vC_0)
print(round(i0_mA, 3))
print(round(vC_t, 2))

traps: Using the source value as the final value of every variable. In an RC step v_C ends at V_s but i_C ends at 0; in an RL step i_L ends at V_s/R but v_L ends at 0.
Putting x(0⁻) into the shortcut for a quantity that jumps at switching. Use x(0⁺); only v_C and i_L are guaranteed continuous.
Forgetting that τ uses the Thévenin resistance seen by C or L after switching, with sources killed.
Dropping the minus sign in the natural part. For a rising step x(0⁺) < x(∞), the natural term x(0⁺) − x(∞) is negative.
Treating a pulse as one step. A pulse has two switching instants; restart the formula at the second one.

quiz.q: State the continuity rule for capacitor voltage and inductor current at a switching instant.
quiz.a: Capacitor voltage cannot jump: v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻). Inductor current cannot jump: i_L(0⁺) = i_L(0⁻).

quiz.q: Why does the natural part of a DC step response decay to zero while the forced part remains?
quiz.a: The natural part solves the source-free equation and has the form A e^(−t/τ), so it decays with τ. The forced part is the particular solution that follows the constant source, so it stays at x(∞).

quiz.q: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 μF, V_s = 5 V, capacitor uncharged. Find τ and v_C(t).
L = 2 H, R = 10 Ω, V_s = 20 V, i(0) = 0. Find τ, i(∞), and i(t).
In the worked example, find i(0⁺) and i(∞). Why does one jump?
quiz.a: i(0⁺) = (10 − 0)/50 kΩ = 0.2 mA. i(∞) = 0 because the capacitor is open to DC. Capacitor current can jump because capacitor voltage cannot; the source suddenly fixes the resistor voltage at t = 0⁺.

quiz.q: Sketch v_C when v_C(0⁺) = 5 V, v_C(∞) = 10 V, τ = 2 s. Give the initial slope and v_C at t = 2 s.
quiz.a: The curve rises from 5 V to 10 V. Initial slope = (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5 V/s. v_C(2) = 10 + (5 − 10)e^(−1) = 8.16 V.

quiz.q: What does x(0⁺) mean in the shortcut formula?
quiz.a: x(0⁺) is the value of the voltage or current immediately after switching, not before. For v_C and i_L it equals the value at 0⁻; for other variables it may be different.

beyond: Not for the exam. SPICE transient analysis solves exactly this exponential update for every capacitor and inductor at each time step, with automatic time-step control near switching. The same first-order curve sets on-chip RC interconnect delay, gate-oxide charging, and the thermal rise of a power device. Search for 'RC delay Elmore', 'SPICE transient integration', or 'first-order thermal model' to go further.
